findings.breaking_input: ARC_ROOT containing a single quote or a backslash, e.g. /tmp/arc'x on POSIX or a Windows path with spaces; probe() runs ( cd "$ARC_ROOT" && node ... ) but $ARC_ROOT is not exported when the bats file runs check_paths and ignored_in_copy in the same process, and the subshell cd with an unquoted variable is actually quoted here, however the native() helper is used for the mutant YAML and verdict paths while the real engine/harnesses.yaml is passed as a relative path after cd, so a path with a space is fine, but a symlinked $ARC_ROOT (macOS /var -> /private/var) makes the probe read the resolved tree while ignored_in_copy and the seed-dir find use the unresolved $ARC_ROOT, so REQ-05's dirty-diff and the seed count read different trees than the probe validated — fixed-defects class (f).
findings.why: probe() cds into $ARC_ROOT and passes a relative path, but the bats assertions read $ARC_ROOT/… and $BATS_TEST_TMPDIR paths directly, so on a symlinked or junctioned checkout the probe validates one tree while the test counts seeds and checks .gitignore against another. The debt ledger B10 fixed this for the verdict mutant arm by passing the same $ARC_ROOT/$v to both, but the real arm still passes a relative path that resolves after cd while the seed dir and .gitignore reads use the absolute $ARC_ROOT. Also the mutant YAML and short.md go through native() while the real .gitignore and verdict go through the relative path, so the two arms resolve differently.
findings.fix: Resolve one canonical realpath for $ARC_ROOT once (native() + realpath -m) and pass the same absolute path to every probe invocation and every bats-side read of the tree.

findings.breaking_input: A row whose verified date is removed but whose status is also removed, or the undated mutant deletes only one verified line so the probe prints fewer than rows undated; but the real hole: the mutant grep -vE '^[[:space:]]+verified: ' strips every indented verified: line including those of unverified rows AND the claude-code row's own verified date, then the assertion requires every row to be undated, which can pass even when the probe's DATE check would have accepted a row that kept its date — because the mutant's stdout line field rows is read from the mutated probe run, and if the mutant deleted a verified line inside golden_transform or a nested value, the probe still counts rows but the assertion demands rows undated, which is exactly the count, so a mutant that strips a non-date verified line is still accepted; but more concretely, the breaking input is a harnesses.yaml where one verified row's verified: is written on the same line as another key in block style (e.g. "verified: "2026-10-07" version: "1.17.18"") — the mutant grep removes part of that line, the probe DATE regex then fails it as undated while the original row is legal, but the assertion only checks that the number of undated equals the number of rows, so the mutant passes even though the check is exercised on a malformed file, not on a real row.
findings.why: The mutant removes every indented verified: line, and the assertion only verifies the count of undated equals the row count — it never verifies that a single, correctly-indented, previously-valid row lost its date. The mutant can instead mangle a nested value or a different indentation and still satisfy the count assertion, meaning the test does not prove the DATE check sees each row's date. Debt ledger 22fddfc B5 claimed "asserts every row is reported" but the count-equals-rows assertion is weaker than proving each row's date was removed.
findings.fix: In the mutant, delete exactly one verified: line from a known valid row, assert the mutant differs by exactly that line (cmp and line-count diff == 1), and assert the probe reports exactly 1 undated while the original reports 0.
findings.twin_of: (s) a mutant whose assertion is weaker than its change

findings.breaking_input: A .gitignore that ignores .codex only via a global core.excludesFile or via .git/info/exclude in the main clone; check_paths runs git with GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null but the temp repo created by ignored_in_copy does not copy .git/info/exclude from the real tree, so a rule that lives in the main clone's .git/info/exclude (not in the committed .gitignore) makes the real check report "git still ignores" while every clean clone is fine — the false failure is acceptable, but the deeper twin: the mutant arm plants .codex/* into a temp repo whose .gitignore is CR-stripped, yet the check_paths function probes .opencode/commands/x.md too, so a real .gitignore that ignores .opencode/ but not .codex passes the real arm, and the mutant only plants .codex/*, so the opencode surface is never mutant-tested.
findings.why: The mutant arm for the ignore check only plants .codex/*, but the real arm probes four rendered paths (.codex, .agents, AGENTS.md, .opencode). A future edit that adds only .opencode/ to .gitignore is caught by the real arm, but the mutant control never proves the check sees a planted .opencode rule — the sole mutant is for .codex, so the opencode probe is never negatively tested and could be deleted from the check without a red. This is class (j) vacuous pass on that surface.
findings.fix: Plant a second mutant that adds .opencode/ and assert the check reports .opencode/commands/x.md as ignored.

findings.breaking_input: A verdict file where the seo-article-writer row is missing and one source-command-arc-* row is duplicated under a case-variant name; the probe's seen set rejects duplicates by exact name, so a duplicate with a different case (source-command-arc-Pr) is counted as illegal, command-rows drops to 7, and 'verdict incomplete' fires — so the set-by-name fix works. But the twin hole: a verdict file that lists 8 command rows all named correctly but where one is FAITHFUL and the matching source command is missing its skill's directory would set faithful=1, and the seeds comparison `[ "$seeds" -eq "$(field faithful)" ]` passes only if a codex-seed dir exists; however the breaking input is a verdict where the seo row is FAITHFUL (legal per the probe: verdict === 'FAITHFUL' is accepted for the seo name) and truly a matching .claude/skills/seo-article-writer exists, but the bats test computes seeds only from codex-seed dirs and compares to faithful which excludes seo — so a FAITHFUL seo-article-writer row would make faithful=0 and seeds=0, test passes, while the probe never verifies that the seo FAITHFUL verdict maps to any real file.
findings.why: The probe accepts FAITHFUL for the seo-article-writer row (the guard `if (name !== "seo-article-writer") faithful += 1` only avoids counting it in faithful), and the seeds comparison only counts codex-seed dirs. A FAITHFUL seo row is therefore never checked against a golden, and the spec's step 2 says a faithful seo is compared and dropped only if tracked — but nothing in the probe or bats verifies the tracked .claude/skills/seo-article-writer exists or that the verdict's FAITHFUL claim is reflected by the expected tracked file. The row is validated as a string but no side of the comparison is ever made.
findings.fix: In the probe, when seo-article-writer is FAITHFUL, also require that the tracked .claude/skills/seo-article-writer/SKILL.md exists (realpath guard) and report a PROBLEM otherwise.

findings.breaking_input: engine/harnesses.yaml where a verified row has verified: absent but status: verified, and the row's version/source are present; the probe's DATE check rejects it as undated, good. But the real twin hole is the converse guard: a row with status: unverified and a falsy verified that happens to be a valid date format is accepted with a date, and the bats test 4 asserts exactly 4 verified rows — an attacker can add a 5th row with status: unverified and verified: "2026-10-07" (a date) and the probe counts it as unverified (verified += 1 only for status === verified), so verified field stays 4, but the DATE check passes on the unverified row because the pattern is applied unconditionally to every row. So a row whose status is unverified but which is dated 2026-10-07 is treated as fully valid, and the matrix can declare an unverified row dated, which per DST-C means "a row without a date does not install" — the check should reject a dated unverified row, not accept it.
findings.why: The DATE regex is applied to r.verified for every row regardless of status, so an unverified row with a date passes the undated check. The contract in harnesses.yaml's header says an unverified row is a declaration that arc has NOT checked that harness, and ADR-2003 says a row without a date does not install — implying an unverified row must NOT be dated. The probe's status-verified count is separate, so the test's exactly-4-verified assertion does not catch a dated unverified row.
findings.fix: When r.status === 'unverified', require that verified is absent or matches no date (or a distinct marker like 'unverified' and reject the DATE pattern); when verified, require the date. Add a mutant that dates an unverified row and assert it acts as illegal.

findings.breaking_input: A verdict row where a cell contains a pipe inside the name, e.g. | source-command-arc-commit|evil | DIVERGED | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 |; the probe splits on every | and takes cells[0] and cells[1], so the name becomes 'source-command-arc-commit' and the verdict 'evil', which is neither DIVERGED nor FAITHFUL so illegal increments, caught. But the true hole: a verdict column containing 'DIVERGED|FAITHFUL' — split gives cells[1]='DIVERGED' so it's legal even though the cell holds two values, and the name cell 'source-command-arc-commit|source-command-arc-ship' produces name 'source-command-arc-commit' with the rest swallowed, so two skills could share a row and the count still be 8.
findings.why: Splitting on every pipe means a pipe inside a name or verdict cell silently changes the classified values; the probe never validates that the raw verdict cell contains exactly FAITHFUL or DIVERGED with no extra pipe, and the set-based name check counts the swallowed prefix as a real row. The spec's own comparison inputs use no internal pipes, so this is a malformed-table silent-accept hole (class m row-shape).
findings.fix: Split on the surrounding pipes only — match the line against a strict ^\| *name *\| *(FAITHFUL|DIVERGED) *\| *[0-9]+ *\| *[0-9]+ *\| *[0-9]+ *\| *[0-9]+ *\|$ and on any other line with a leading pipe, increment illegal.

findings.breaking_input: engine/harnesses.yaml where a partial cell value is exactly 'partial:' with no note, e.g. hooks: "partial:"; the cell regex is /^partial:\S/, which requires a non-space character after the colon, so 'partial:' alone fails — good. But the twin hole is 'partial: ' followed by a space then a note: the regex requires \S immediately after the colon, so 'partial: note' (with the space the spec's note format uses) fails and the cell is illegal, while the spec declares cells partial like 'partial: plugin tool.execute.before' with a space. The committed file uses 'partial:rendered as skills at ...' without a space, but the ADR 2003 cell format is 'partial:<note>' with no space, so the committed one matches — however a future editor writing the natural 'partial: ' with a space would be rejected even though it's semantically identical. That's a logic false-negative, not a security hole. The actual hole is the inverse: 'partial:x\ny' where the note contains a newline — the regex only checks the first character after the colon, so a partial cell whose note is one line but whose value object got a trailing key can slip.
findings.why: The partial regex validates only the first non-space char after the colon, not the whole cell, and the parser read one value while the regex re-reads it — validate-one-read-compare-another on the cell shape. More concretely: the probe never rejects a cell that is 'true' or 'false' string with surrounding whitespace trimmed away by the YAML subset parser, so a cell written as " true " is legal, and the matrix's 'true'/'false' contract that install places only true cells is then decided by the parser's trim behavior rather than the declared bytes.
findings.fix: For each cell, require the raw value to be exactly 'true', exactly 'false', or to start with 'partial:' followed by at least one non-whitespace character and contain no newline; and assert the value's first character is not a space.

findings.breaking_input: The seed-dir count: `[ "$seeds" -eq "$(field faithful)" ]` — the probe counts faithful command rows where verdict === 'FAITHFUL' and name !== 'seo-article-writer', and the bats counts codex-seed subdirectories. The breaking input is a verdict file with a FAITHFUL row and the matching codex-seed dir present, but the dir name is a different skill (e.g. two FAITHFUL rows, one seed dir with the wrong name) — the counts still match, so the seed set is never verified against the names of the FAITHFUL rows. The spec said faithful files are copied to tests/fixtures/distribute/goldens/codex-seed/<n>/SKILL.md, so a misplaced seed dir could satisfy the count with the wrong content.
findings.why: Only the dir count is compared to the FAITHFUL count, never the dir names against the FAITHFUL row names. This is a derived-set check (k) that reads the count but not the set, so a wrong-named seed dir or a genuine FAITHFUL row with no dir but a compensating extra dir passes. With 0 FAITHFUL on 2026-10-07 the check is vacuous too, but the structural hole stands.
findings.fix: Collect the list of FAITHFUL command names from the probe (print them) and assert the set of codex-seed dir names equals that set exactly.

findings.breaking_input: A verdict file where the only change is the deleted pr row is moved to the bottom of the table with a header line and the same 8 rows; the mutant grep deletes the pr row wherever it sits and the probe reports incomplete — fine. But the mutant arm uses grep -vE '^[|][[:space:]]*source-command-arc-pr[[:space:]]*[|]' and the cmp guard only checks the file changed, not that exactly one row was removed; if a future verdict table had a second row whose name is 'source-command-arc-pr ' (with a trailing space) the grep also removes it, the probe reports 'illegal' because the seen set now lacks a real name and the count drops to 7, and the assertion still correctly sees incomplete — so it fails for the right reason. The actual hole is that the real arm and the mutant arm both assert the same 'verdict incomplete' string, so a broken probe that always printed verdict incomplete would pass both; the probe's only differing output is the RAN marker and the counts, and the counts are never asserted in the mutant arm.
findings.why: The mutant arm asserts only that the probe prints 'verdict incomplete', never that the FAITHFUL count or command-rows changed specifically. A probe that conflates any legal-row missing with 'incomplete' (including an illegal-header case) satisfies the mutant, and the bats test 7's real arm also only greps 'verdict complete', so the two arms share the same weak assertion — a mutant (deleted row) is not distinguished from a malformed table. This is class (s): the mutant's assertion is weaker than its change.
findings.fix: In the mutant arm, after the probe run, assert field command-rows equals 7 (or print the counts and compare to the real run's), not just the 'verdict incomplete' grep.
findings.twin_of: (s) a mutant whose assertion is weaker than its change

findings.breaking_input: The exactly-4-verified-rows assertion uses `[ "$(field verified)" -eq 4 ]` with no POSIX -ge guard on the probe stderr; but the real hole: the field extraction uses sed -n "s/^verified //p" where the value is 'verified 5' — if a future edit adds a fifth verified row, the test fails red, good. But the breaking input is a verified row whose version or source value contains a newline (block YAML folded): the probe prints 'no version' as a PROBLEM and the has_problem guard catches it, but the exactly-4 assertion passes regardless of the PROBLEM lines, so a verified row missing its version is only caught if has_problem's pattern matches; the has_problem regex is '.*: (undated|no version|no source)$' and a PROBLEM line like 'x: no version' matches, so it's caught. The weakness is the inverse: NO has_problem line is checked for the forbidden 'no version' across all rows — only the exact-4 count and the undated regex, so a verified row whose version key is present but empty string passes the probe's typeof check (trim() === '' fails, so it's caught) — actually the probe catches it, so no hole there. The real hole is test 5's `cells -eq rows*9` where cellsChecked counts only cells present; a row with all 9 cells plus an unknown cell increments cellsChecked for the 9 and adds a PROBLEM, so cells == rows*9 and the has_problem '' guard catches the unknown cell — good. The genuine hole: has_problem '' with grep patterns as arithmetic parameters — grep -E "^PROBLEM " would also match 'PROBLEM ' with a trailing newline in CRLF output stripped by tr, so it's safe.
findings.why: Trace: test 5's cells==rows*9 and has_problem are jointly sufficient; test 4's verified==4 plus undated regex catches missing dates but the probe also raises PROBLEM for a duplicate id, and has_problem in test 4 greps only for undated|no version|no source, so a duplicate-id row with a valid date passes test 4's has_problem guard (the guard returns non-empty only for those three) — the duplicate id is a PROBLEM line but test 4 never checks it; the matrix test 5's has_problem '' would catch it, but test 4 runs first and a duplicate-id row is a different failure class the test claims to cover via the probe. Test 4 is not the issue; the issue is the probe's duplicate-id detection is never asserted by any bats test that requires the duplicate to fail — test 5's has_problem '' will see the PROBLEM line and fail, so it is caught, but only because test 5 runs after test 4; a CI that reordered tests would still run test 5. So no actual defect in duplicate detection. The concrete finding: test 4's has_problem pattern uses a bare '.*' before the alternatives, so PROBLEM 'x: undated: extra' (a date plus trailing text) matches and fails the test, a false positive — but that's fragile, not dangerous.
findings.fix: Split test 4 into one assertion per required field on a per-row basis from the probe's row-by-row output rather than relying on aggregate PROBLEM greps; and in test 4's has_problem, anchor to '^PROBLEM .*: (undated|no version|no source)$' with no leading '.*'.

findings.breaking_input: The real v unused variable: check_paths is passed "$ARC_ROOT" and in the real arm `run check_paths "$ARC_ROOT"` — the function then does git -C "$repo" check-ignore; but the mutant arm calls ignored_in_copy which creates a new temp repo and does not copy .git/info/exclude, .gitattributes, or core.excludesFile from the real tree; so if the real .gitignore relies on a nested .git/info/exclude inside the repo's .git directory (which a user could set for the main clone), the real check sees paths ignored and fails red, while CI clones are clean — a machine-decides-the-answer false failure. That is not a security hole but the earlier B2 fix claimed GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL neutralization; global excludesFile is neutralized but $HOME/.config/git/ignore and init.templateDir with a template info/exclude are not neutralized because git init without --template= copies the template dir's info/exclude into the temp .git — so on a machine with a template containing 'AGENTS.md', the mutant temp repo ignores AGENTS.md and the mutant arm's check reports AGENTS.md ignored (passes), and the real arm on a clean machine reports clean — the check passes on both but for different reasons, and a machine that has init.templateDir with .codex would make the real arm fail, while CI passes.
findings.why: ignored_in_copy runs git init without --template=, so a user's init.templateDir can pre-seed info/exclude rules into the temp repo, making the mutant or real arm decide the answer by machine. The fixed-defects record (r) claims GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null handles ambient git, but init.templateDir is read regardless of those env vars. The real arm checks the real .gitignore but the temp repo the mutant uses has ambient template state, so a machine with a template ignoring .codex makes the mutant arm's check report .codex/hooks.json as ignored — the mutant assertion expects lines[0] to be .codex/hooks.json, so it still passes for the right reason only if the template ignores .codex; a template ignoring .agents instead would make lines[0] .agents and the mutant assertion fails wrongly.
findings.fix: Run git init --template= for the temp repo (and add GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM alongside the existing globals).

findings.breaking_input: engine/harnesses.yaml with a row whose golden is 'tests/fixtures/../engine/harnesses.yaml' — the confinement regex /\\|:|(^|\/)\.\.(\/|$)/ rejects the .. segment — good. But the twin hole is a golden value with a trailing slash or a leading './': './tests/fixtures/x/' passes the startsWith 'tests/fixtures/' check? No, startsWith fails for './'. 'tests/fixtures//x' passes and 'tests/fixtures/..' — the regex rejects .. followed by a slash or end, so 'tests/fixtures/..foo' does not match the .. detection (the regex requires a (^|/) before '..' and (/) or $ after, so 'tests/fixtures/..foo' has '..' followed by 'f' — no match, passes; 'tests/fixtures/..' followed by end matches and is rejected). So 'tests/fixtures/..foo' is accepted as a confined path even though resolving it yields 'tests/fixtures/..foo' which is outside the directory in the sense the name is misleading but it stays under tests/fixtures/ literally. That is not a traversal. The real hole is the probe validates the golden string but the P03 installer later reads it from the same parsed file — the path is stored and used, so validate-one-read holds. But the cell check has a separate path: the probe reads the file, parses it, and validates; the bats test reads the same file via field claude-golden from the probe output — so the bytes are compared to the probe's own output, and the probe prints cc.golden || '(none)' with no normalization, so a golden value with a trailing space in the YAML (parser trims?) is printed without the space and the bats comparison passes while the installer reads the untrimmed value from the file.
findings.why: The probe prints the parsed golden value, and the bats test compares that printed value to the string, but the installer will read the file directly — so the validated string and the used string can differ on whitespace or escape handling by the subset parser, while the probe never validates the raw bytes of the golden cell against the parsed value. This is a validate-one-read-compare-another instance (f) for the golden (the very thing class (f) exists to catch).
findings.fix: Have the probe read the raw YAML line for the golden and assert the raw trimmed equals the parsed value before printing; and print the raw byte length so the bats test can pin it.

findings.breaking_input: The seeds==faithful comparison runs before `run --separate-stderr probe verdict "$v"` in the test body; the test uses the earlier `run` from the real probe to print output, and then the mutant run overwrites $output, but the seeds comparison uses $(field faithful) which reads $output from the LAST run — which is the mutant probe run, so when the real arm's faithful is 0 and the mutant run's output has command-rows 7 but faithful might still be 0 (if the deleted row was DIVERGED), the seeds comparison after the mutant run compares seeds (from the real tree) to the mutant's faithful (still 0) — a no-op. The order reads: real probe runs, checks verdict complete, computes seeds from real tree, compares seeds to $(field faithful) — this is before the mutant, so it uses the real run's $output. Then the mutant greps, checks cmp, runs mutant probe, and only then asserts verdict incomplete. So the faithful comparison is correct. The real hole: the seeds count uses find over codex-seed WITHOUT asserting the RAN of the find (a missing codex-seed dir yields 0 seeds and 0 faithful — vacuous). The spec says 0 of 8 are faithful on 2026-10-07, so seeds==0==faithful passes with no actual check that the verdict's faithful count is separately validated against any directory.
findings.why: When faithful is 0 (as in the committed tree), the seeds==faithful assertion compares 0 to 0 with no negative control proving the check would fail if a seed dir existed — a seed dir that the spec would require for a FAITHFUL row is not tested because no fixture plants one and asserts the count flips. Class (j) vacuous pass.
findings.fix: Add a mutant arm that plants one codex-seed dir with a matching FAITHFUL verdict row and asserts seeds==1, and a second that plants a seed dir with no FAITHFUL row and asserts the comparison fails.

findings.breaking_input: The probe reads file with readFileSync(file, 'utf8') after only checking the file exists and is non-empty; if the file is a symlink to another file, read follows it, and the bats side reads the same $ARC_ROOT path without realpath, so the symlinked and real trees can differ — already covered by L1's symlink finding; the distinct hole: the probe reads read(file) where file is argv[3]; the bats side passes a relative path after cd for the real arm and a native() absolute path for mutants — the real arm's relative path is resolved against cwd=$ARC_ROOT, but bats also sets BATS_TEST_TMPDIR and the native() path is absolute, so a symlink resolution mismatch is only for $ARC_ROOT, which the probe's import URL and the bats reads share. The concrete breaking input for class (g): $ARC_ROOT contains a space AND the mutant path goes through cygpath -m, which on MSYS converts /tmp/... to C:/msys/... but $BATS_TEST_TMPDIR may itself contain a space or a non-ASCII char; cygpath -m leaves the rest, node opens it fine; no bug. The real issue: on Windows, native() with cygpath -m returns a C:/ drive path, but the probe's import(new URL(../../.claude/scripts/engine/yaml-subset.mjs, import.meta.url)) from a file located under tests/ works, yet the file being probed (undated.yaml) is in $BATS_TEST_TMPDIR which cygpath -m makes C:/... — fine. So the only real class-(g) instance is the probe's own location: if $ARC_ROOT is a native Windows path (not MSYS), the relative '../.claude/...' import resolves fine. No concrete defect.
findings.why: No concrete defect reachable in this diff — the (g) class was already fixed via native() and the relative-cd pattern.
findings.fix: None — fold this into the L1 symlink resolution finding

findings.breaking_input: check_paths's real arm runs git check-ignore without --no-index on an absolute repo path but the path is never created — the file .codex/hooks.json need not exist for check-ignore to answer, and --no-index forces git to consider the path even if it does not exist, so this is fine; the concrete hole is that the real arm's check asks whether .opencode/commands/x.md is ignored, but the rendered opencode directory may have different plural paths per the live docs (.opencode/commands/ vs .opencode/command/) and ADR-2010 says P00 confirms paths; probing .opencode/commands/x.md before confirmation can give a false clean if the actual rendered path is .opencode/command/x.md and the ignore rule only matches the singular — but the check is about whether ANY rendered surface is gitignored, and a rule ignoring .opencode/command/ without .opencode/commands/ would be missed. The probe's fixed set is hard-coded and not derived from harnesses.yaml, so a new rendered surface row added later (Hermes row) is never probed by this test, and the fixed-defects class (k) derived-not-hand-kept applies.
findings.why: The four probed paths are hard-coded in check_paths, not derived from the harnesses.yaml golden/rendered directories, so a new harness row or a corrected plural path (ADR-2010 P00 corrections) is never covered by test 2's ignore check; the check is hand-kept and silently drifts.
findings.fix: Derive the probed paths from the matrix rows' rendered-dir naming convention, or at least read .opencode/commands vs /command from the live confirmation and feed it into check_paths.
